h1: Aglio e Olio Recipe: Spaghetti with Garlic, Chilli and Olive Oil
excerpt: The four-ingredient version by weight and volume, for two and for four, with the pasta-water step that turns oil into sauce and the point past which garlic ruins the plate.
keyTakeaway: Aglio e olio is spaghetti, garlic, chilli and extra virgin olive oil bound with starchy pasta water. Weigh the pasta, take the garlic only as far as blond, keep a mugful of the cooking water back, and stir the last third of the oil in raw off the heat.

intro: Aglio e olio exposes a kitchen: four ingredients, twelve minutes, nothing on the plate to hide behind.
Two things separate a good bowl from an oily one: the pasta water, and how far the garlic went.

sections.heading: The four ingredients, by weight and volume

blocks.text: Spaghetti, garlic, chilli and extra virgin olive oil, finished with parsley and a ladle of the water the pasta cooked in. With so few components, quantities matter more here than in a dish of fifteen. Weigh the pasta and measure the oil.

sections.heading: How to make aglio olio, step by step

blocks.text: Everything happens in the time the spaghetti takes, so slice the garlic and chop the parsley before the water boils. The method below runs pan and pot in parallel and brings them together while both are hot, the only moment a sauce will form.

items: Boil 2 litres of water, salted with 20 g — double every quantity in this method for four. It should taste clearly salty.
Slice the garlic thin by hand; chopped garlic burns, slices cook evenly.
Drop the spaghetti, timer set one minute short of the packet time.
With about five minutes left on the pasta, put 40 ml of oil and the garlic in a **cold** wide pan over low heat.
When the edges turn pale gold, about four minutes, add the chilli and pull the pan off.
Keep a mugful of cooking water back, drain, and lift the spaghetti across; add a ladle, 120 ml, of that water.
Back on medium heat, toss hard for 60 to 90 seconds until the liquid clings.
Off the heat, stir in parsley and the last 20 ml of oil raw. Serve immediately.

sections.heading: The pasta water step people get wrong

blocks.text: The sauce is an emulsion. Starch dissolved in the cooking water holds oil and water together so the mixture coats every strand instead of pooling under it. Two habits break it: draining into a colander and losing that water, and finishing the toss off the heat.

items: **Keep a mugful back** before draining. It is the only thickener here.
**Undercook by two minutes.** The rest happens in the pan.
**Toss, do not stir.** Agitation forces oil and water to combine.
**Judge by the pan,** not the clock: ready when it turns glossy.

blocks.text: Garlic in warm oil travels from raw to sweet to bitter fast, and brown garlic ruins the plate because the oil carries that bitterness into every strand. Blond is the target: pale gold at the edges, still soft in the middle, smelling sweet. A cold start buys time.

items: **A few dark edges?** Off the heat at once, lift those slices out.
**Brown and smelling acrid?** Start over. Four minutes against a bitter dinner.
**Burning every time?** Use a wider pan: one layer cooks evenly.

sections.heading: Chilli, parsley and the second pour

blocks.text: The chilli is warmth, not fire: one dried chilli crumbled, or half a teaspoon of flakes, for two. Parsley goes in off the heat so it stays green. The oil arrives twice, warm at the start to carry the garlic, cold at the end for the aroma heat drives off.
Two-thirds of the oil cooks, one-third goes in raw. That last 20 ml is most of what you smell.

sections.heading: Mostly oil, so the oil is the flavour

blocks.text: Strip the recipe back and it is pasta, garlic and about 30 ml of oil a head. Nothing else carries the plate. A flat refined oil makes a flat bowl: texture and salt, no fruit. This is the dish where an extra virgin's pepper and grassiness has somewhere to go.

A young, green, peppery oil suits it: bitterness that is aggressive off a spoon becomes backbone against starch. Heat is not the constraint here — [what heat olive oil takes](/blog/olive-oil-smoke-point-what-heat-it-can-take) covers that. [Arabian Village](/products) sells it in 250 ml and 500 ml.
Salt the water, keep a mugful back, start the garlic in cold oil and stop at blond, toss until glossy, then stir a third of the oil in raw.

faqs.q: How much olive oil goes into aglio olio?
faqs.a: About 30 ml of extra virgin olive oil per 100 g of dried spaghetti, so 60 ml for two. Use two-thirds warm with the garlic and stir the last third in raw.

faqs.q: Why is my aglio olio oily instead of glossy?
faqs.a: The oil and the pasta water never emulsified. Add a ladle of starchy cooking water, put the pan back over medium heat, and toss hard for a minute until the liquid clings.

faqs.q: Can I use ordinary olive oil instead of extra virgin?
faqs.a: You can, and the bowl will be duller. Nearly all the flavour here comes from the oil and the garlic, so a refined oil leaves texture and salt without fruit or pepper.

faqs.q: What do I do if the garlic turns brown?
faqs.a: If only a few edges caught, lift the pan off the heat and remove the darkest slices. If it smells acrid, start the garlic again in fresh oil: brown garlic turns everything bitter.

faqs.q: Should aglio e olio have cheese in it?
faqs.a: The classic version has none and the sauce holds without it. Grated hard cheese at the table is common outside Italy; add it off the heat, or it clumps instead of melting.

faqs.q: How long does aglio olio take to make?
faqs.a: Roughly the time the spaghetti boils, about twelve minutes, plus five to slice garlic and chop parsley. Prepare everything before the pasta goes in, because the finish itself takes only ninety seconds.
